topics.title: Introduction and Purpose of Capital Budgeting
explain: Capital budgeting involves planning and evaluating long-term capital investments.
It aims at optimum utilization of funds to maximize shareholder wealth.
Decisions involve substantial financial outlays with effects spanning many years.
Most capital investments are irreversible without heavy financial losses.
They are complex because they require forecasting uncertain future cash flows.

flow.title: Capital Budgeting Core Tasks
steps: Identify strategic investment opportunities
Forecast after-tax incremental cash flows
Evaluate project returns and risks
Select proposal maximizing owner wealth

topics.example: A bakery deciding whether to spend money on buying a commercial automated oven that will last 10 years.
remember: Capital budgeting deals with long-term, irreversible decisions involving substantial funds.
mistakes: Confusing short-term operational expenditure budgeting with long-term capital investment appraisal.

quiz.q: Why are capital budgeting decisions generally considered irreversible?
o: Due to upfront costs and contractual obligations
Because government regulations forbid closing down projects
Because accounting standards do not permit asset sales
Due to compulsory depreciation requirements
quiz.why: Huge upfront payments and contractual obligations make reversal difficult and economically unfeasible.

quiz.q: What is the primary objective of capital investment decisions?
o: Minimizing current year tax outflow
Maximizing the wealth of the organization and shareholders
Increasing immediate accounting profits
Achieving maximum short-term sales volume
quiz.why: Capital budgeting aims to maximize firm value and shareholder wealth over the long term.

topics.title: Capital Budgeting Process
explain: The process starts by identifying potential investment ideas matching business strategy.
Identified proposals enter the evaluation phase to estimate cash flows and test feasibility.
Selected projects are chosen based on wealth maximization and organizational cost of capital.
During implementation, assets are procured and funds are allocated to start operations.
Control monitors real progress via feedback reports, followed by post-completion reviews.

flow.title: Stages in Capital Budgeting Process
steps: Identify potential investment opportunities
Evaluate proposals using appraisal techniques
Select optimal project maximizing wealth
Acquire funds and implement project
Monitor progress through control reports
Conduct post-completion review and feedback

topics.example: A retail chain spots a new mall location, estimates traffic and costs, gets board approval, constructs the store, tracks weekly sales, and assesses success after year one.
remember: The 6 phases are Planning, Evaluation, Selection, Implementation, Control, and Review.
mistakes: Skipping the review phase, which is critical to learn whether past forecasts matched actuals.

quiz.q: Which stage in the capital budgeting process directly compares actual performance against plans?
o: Evaluation
Selection
Control
Planning
quiz.why: Control monitors ongoing execution with progress reports and compares actual performance against planned targets.

quiz.q: What is the main activity during the evaluation stage?
o: Drafting legal purchase agreements
Appraising cash inflows and outflows using decision models
Conducting post-completion audits
Floating shares in the capital market
quiz.why: The evaluation phase appraises the expected cash inflows and outflows using financial techniques.

topics.title: Types of Capital Investment Decisions
explain: On the basis of firm existence, projects are for new firms or existing firms.
Existing firms face replacement and modernization (cost reduction) or expansion and diversification (revenue expansion).
On the basis of situation, mutually exclusive proposals mean accepting one rejects all others.
Accept-reject decisions apply to independent projects meeting a hurdle cut-off rate.
Contingent decisions occur when investing in one project demands mandatory investment in another.

flow.title: Classification of Investment Decisions
steps: Classify by existence or decision situation
Assess if proposals compete with each other
Identify independent or mutually exclusive nature
Check for dependent contingent capital commitments

topics.example: Deciding between buying a diesel generator or a solar grid is mutually exclusive; building a remote factory requiring employee housing is a contingent decision.
remember: Replacement/Modernization = Cost reduction; Expansion/Diversification = Revenue expansion.
mistakes: Treating mutually exclusive projects like independent projects and accepting multiple competing options simultaneously.

quiz.q: Decisions where the acceptance of one proposal excludes the acceptance of others are known as:
o: Contingent decisions
Mutually exclusive decisions
Independent decisions
Diversification decisions
quiz.why: Mutually exclusive alternatives compete directly, so choosing one automatically excludes the other.

quiz.q: Investment proposals aimed at modernizing outdated machinery to reduce costs are called:
o: Revenue expansion decisions
Cost reduction decisions
Contingent decisions
Divisible project decisions
quiz.why: Replacement and modernization decisions focus primarily on enhancing operational efficiency and lowering operating costs.

topics.title: Estimation of Cash Flows and Basic Principles
explain: Appraisal must use incremental after-tax cash flows rather than accounting profits.
Depreciation is a non-cash expense that generates a cash inflow via tax shield.
Financing costs like interest and dividends are excluded from cash flows to avoid double counting with WACC.
Sunk costs are past unrecoverable outlays and must be ignored in decision making.
Opportunity costs of existing assets used and working capital requirements must be included.

flow.title: Deriving Cash Inflow After Tax (CFAT)
steps: Start with operating revenue less operating cash costs
Deduct tax depreciation to find EBT
Subtract corporate income tax to get EAT
Add back tax depreciation to arrive at CFAT

topics.example: If buying a machine saves Rs. 10,000 depreciation tax shield, that saving is an incremental cash inflow, while Rs. 50,000 spent on feasibility study last year is ignored as a sunk cost.
remember: Tax shield on depreciation = Depreciation × Tax Rate.
Initial working capital is an outflow at Year 0 and fully recovered as an inflow at the project end.
mistakes: Deducting interest expense from project cash flows when discounting by the WACC.

quiz.q: Why are financing costs like interest excluded when defining project cash flows?
o: Because interest is non-deductible under income tax laws
Because interest is already reflected in the weighted average cost of capital discount rate
Because capital budgeting only considers equity investments
Because interest charges cannot be accurately forecasted
quiz.why: Cost of capital reflects debt and equity financing charges; deducting them from cash flows counts them twice.

quiz.q: How is initial working capital treated across the life of a capital project?
o: Depreciated over the asset useful life
Treated as initial cash outflow and terminal cash inflow upon release
Ignored because it does not represent fixed assets
Written off immediately against Year 1 profits
quiz.why: Working capital committed at the start is an initial outflow and is recovered at project completion as an inflow.

topics.title: Block of Assets and Tax Depreciation Rules
explain: Tax depreciation follows the concept of 'Block of Assets' under the Income Tax Act.
If a block contains only one asset and is sold at project end, the block ceases to exist.
Any shortfall between WDV and sale price in a single-asset block is Short Term Capital Loss (STCL), generating tax benefit.
If multiple assets remain in the block, salvage is deducted from WDV and depreciation continues on the remaining pool.
When salvage exceeds the opening WDV in a multi-asset block, depreciation stops and capital gains arise.

flow.title: Terminal Tax Impact on Asset Disposal
steps: Determine opening WDV of the asset block
Check if block ceases to exist or continues
Deduct net salvage proceeds from opening WDV
Compute terminal depreciation or STCL / STCG tax effect

topics.example: A machine with WDV Rs. 40,960 is sold for Rs. 10,000 at Year 5. In a single-asset block, STCL is Rs. 30,960 giving a 30% tax saving of Rs. 9,288.
remember: Single-asset block cessation: calculate STCL/STCG tax shield.
Continuing block: deduct sale value and charge regular depreciation on balance WDV.
mistakes: Charging normal depreciation in Year 5 when the block ceases to exist upon selling the only asset.

quiz.q: When a single asset in a block is sold and the block ceases to exist, what happens if salvage value is less than opening WDV?
o: Normal depreciation continues indefinitely
Short Term Capital Loss arises, yielding a tax shield
The loss is capitalized into goodwill
Short Term Capital Gain arises
quiz.why: Under Income Tax rules, the difference between WDV and scrap value is treated as STCL when the block ceases.

quiz.q: In a continuing block of assets with multiple machines, how is the sale proceeds of an old machine treated?
o: It is credited to the P&L account directly as extraordinary income
It is deducted from the written down value of the block before charging depreciation
It is ignored for tax depreciation purposes
It is subjected to flat 50% capital gains tax immediately
quiz.why: Sale proceeds are subtracted from the block's opening WDV, and depreciation is charged on the residual amount.

topics.title: Payback Period and Payback Reciprocal
explain: Payback period is the time required to recover the initial capital outlay from cash inflows.
For uniform inflows, Payback Period equals Initial Outlay divided by Annual Cash Inflow.
For uneven flows, cumulative cash flows are tracked until total outlay is reached.
It ignores the time value of money and all cash flows generated after the payback period.
Payback reciprocal (Annual Inflow / Initial Investment) approximates IRR if asset life is at least twice the payback period.

flow.title: Calculating Payback for Non-Uniform Inflows
steps: List after-tax cash flows year by year
Compute cumulative cash inflows over time
Identify the year when cumulative flow nears outlay
Add unrecovered fraction: Unrecovered Balance / Year Cash Flow

topics.example: An investment of Rs. 2,00,000 returning Rs. 80,000, Rs. 60,000, and Rs. 60,000 in years 1 to 3 has an exact payback period of 3 years.
remember: Decision rule: Accept if Payback Period <= Target Cut-off Period.
Payback reciprocal = Annual Cash Inflow / Initial Investment.
mistakes: Using accounting profit after depreciation instead of CFAT to calculate payback period.

quiz.q: What is a major limitation of the traditional payback period method?
o: It is too complicated to calculate manually
It ignores the time value of money and cash flows beyond payback
It cannot evaluate projects with uniform cash flows
It requires knowledge of the exact market cost of equity
quiz.why: Payback period treats cash flows equally regardless of timing and disregards all earnings after full capital recovery.

quiz.q: When does the payback reciprocal provide a close approximation of the project's IRR?
o: When the salvage value exceeds 50% of cost
When project life is at least twice the payback period with uniform inflows
When discount rate is equal to zero
When cash flows occur only in the first two years
quiz.why: Payback reciprocal approximates IRR if cash inflows are uniform and the life is at least twice the payback period.

topics.title: Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)
explain: ARR evaluates a project using accounting profits rather than cash flows.
It expresses average annual net income after tax as a percentage of capital investment.
Investment base can be Initial Investment or Average Investment over asset life.
Average Investment is calculated as: 1/2(Initial Cost - Salvage) + Salvage + Additional Working Capital.
Like payback, ARR completely ignores the time value of money and is sensitive to depreciation accounting methods.

flow.title: Computing ARR on Average Investment
steps: Calculate average annual PAT over project life
Compute Average Investment = (Cost - Salvage)/2 + Salvage
Add any additional working capital to base
Divide Average PAT by Average Investment and multiply by 100

topics.example: If a project has an average annual PAT of Rs. 80,000 and average investment of Rs. 1,95,000, the ARR is 80,000 / 1,95,000 = 41.03%.
remember: ARR uses Accounting Profit After Tax (PAT), not CFAT.
Average Investment = 1/2 (Cost - Salvage) + Salvage + Additional Working Capital.
mistakes: Adding depreciation back to income when computing ARR; ARR strictly requires net accounting income.

quiz.q: What numerator is used when computing the Accounting Rate of Return?
o: Average annual cash inflow after tax
Average annual net accounting income after tax
Gross operating profit before depreciation
Terminal year cash flow
quiz.why: ARR uses average annual accounting profit after tax (PAT) across the asset's life.

quiz.q: An asset costs Rs. 1,00,000 with a salvage value of Rs. 20,000. What is the average investment without working capital?

topics.title: Net Present Value (NPV) Technique
explain: NPV is a discounted cash flow technique that accounts for the time value of money.
It discounts all future expected cash inflows and outflows to present values using the cost of capital.
NPV equals the Present Value of Cash Inflows minus the Present Value of Cash Outflows.
An investment proposal is acceptable if NPV is greater than or equal to zero.
For mutually exclusive proposals, the project with the highest positive NPV is chosen.

flow.title: Steps to Determine NPV
steps: Estimate incremental CFAT for each year
Identify appropriate hurdle rate (cost of capital)
Multiply cash flows by relevant PV discount factors
Sum all present values of inflows
Deduct PV of initial and subsequent outflows

topics.example: A project requiring Rs. 1,00,000 today yields discounted inflows of Rs. 1,27,340 over 3 years; its NPV is positive Rs. 27,340, so accept it.
remember: Decision rule: If NPV >= 0, accept; if NPV < 0, reject.
NPV directly measures the dollar/rupee addition to shareholder wealth.
mistakes: Using pre-tax cash flows with post-tax discount rates or mixing nominal cash flows with real rates.

quiz.q: Under the Net Present Value rule, an independent investment proposal should be accepted if:
o: NPV < 0
NPV >= 0
NPV equals initial outlay
Discount factor is greater than 1
quiz.why: A project is accepted if NPV >= 0 because it generates returns equal to or exceeding the cost of capital.

quiz.q: Which of the following is considered a primary theoretical advantage of the NPV method?
o: It ignores cash flows generated in initial years
It assumes cash flows are reinvested at the cost of capital
It gives a percentage rate directly comparable with bank interest
It does not require estimation of a discount rate
quiz.why: NPV's assumption that intermediate cash flows can be reinvested at the cost of capital is realistic and sound.

topics.title: Profitability Index (PI) / Desirability Factor
explain: Profitability Index is the ratio of present value of cash inflows to present value of initial outlay.
It provides a relative measure of project profitability per rupee invested.
A project is accepted if its Profitability Index is greater than or equal to 1.0.
PI is especially valuable when ranking projects under capital rationing with divisible projects.
In mutually exclusive situations with equal NPV, the project with the higher PI is preferred.

flow.title: Evaluating Projects Using PI
steps: Calculate PV of all expected cash inflows
Calculate PV of initial capital outlay
Compute PI = PV of Inflows / PV of Outflows
Accept if PI >= 1; Reject if PI < 1

topics.example: If a project has PV of inflows of Rs. 6,50,000 and initial outlay of Rs. 5,50,000, PI = 6,50,000 / 5,50,000 = 1.18 (Accept).
remember: PI = PV of Cash Inflows / PV of Cash Outflows.
Accept if PI >= 1, Reject if PI < 1.
mistakes: Using undiscounted cash flows in the numerator when calculating PI.

quiz.q: What does a Profitability Index (PI) of 1.25 indicate?
o: The project loses 25% of its capital
Present value of inflows is 1.25 times the initial cash outlay
Accounting rate of return is 25%
Payback occurs in 1.25 years
quiz.why: PI is the ratio of PV of inflows to PV of outflows; 1.25 means PV of inflows exceeds outlay by 25%.

quiz.q: Between two projects with identical positive NPV, how does PI guide choice?
o: Choose the project with the lower PI
Choose the project with the higher PI because it requires less capital per rupee of return
Reject both projects
Both must be chosen regardless of available capital
quiz.why: A higher PI indicates superior capital efficiency, earning more present value per unit of capital invested.

topics.title: Internal Rate of Return (IRR) Method
explain: IRR is the discount rate that makes the Net Present Value of a project equal to zero.
At IRR, the present value of expected cash inflows equals the initial investment outlay.
For even flows, approximate payback is matched in the PVAF table to find the rate.
For uneven flows, IRR is found through trial and error combined with linear interpolation.
A project is accepted if its IRR is greater than or equal to the cost of capital (cut-off rate).

flow.title: IRR Interpolation Procedure
steps: Select discount rate yielding positive NPV (LR)
Select discount rate yielding negative NPV (HR)
Calculate NPV at LR and NPV at HR
Apply formula: LR + [NPV_LR / (NPV_LR - NPV_HR)] * (HR - LR)

remember: At IRR, PV of Inflows = PV of Outflows (NPV = 0).
Decision rule: Accept if IRR >= Cut-off Rate (WACC).
mistakes: Adding negative NPV instead of subtracting it in the denominator of the interpolation formula.

quiz.q: The Internal Rate of Return is precisely that discount rate at which:
o: Accounting profit equals zero
Net Present Value is zero
Profitability Index is zero
Payback period is minimized
quiz.why: By definition, IRR is the discount rate where discounted cash inflows equal discounted outflows, making NPV = 0.

quiz.q: If a project has an IRR of 14% and the company's cost of capital is 11%, the project should be:
o: Rejected
Accepted
Postponed indefinitely
Re-evaluated using ARR only
quiz.why: Projects with IRR greater than the hurdle rate (cut-off rate/WACC) are accepted.

topics.title: NPV vs IRR: Conflicts and Reinvestment Assumptions
explain: NPV and IRR can give conflicting rankings for mutually exclusive projects.
Conflicts arise due to scale disparity (size), time disparity (cash flow pattern), or unequal project lives.
NPV assumes interim cash inflows are reinvested at the company's cost of capital.
IRR implicitly assumes cash flows are reinvested at the project's own internal rate of return.
When rankings conflict, the NPV criterion must be followed because it aligns with shareholder wealth maximization.

flow.title: Resolving NPV vs IRR Ranking Conflict
steps: Identify mutually exclusive proposals
Compute NPV at company cost of capital
Compute IRR for each project
Check for ranking conflict between methods
Select the project with the highest positive NPV

topics.example: Project A requires Rs. 1 lakh with IRR 50% (NPV Rs. 36,360). Project B requires Rs. 5 lakh with IRR 25% (NPV Rs. 68,180). Project B is selected because it creates more absolute wealth.
remember: NPV reinvestment assumption (at WACC) is realistic.
IRR reinvestment assumption (at IRR) is often unrealistic.
Always rely on NPV in case of conflict.
mistakes: Blindly selecting a project with a higher IRR when a mutually exclusive alternative adds significantly more absolute NPV.

quiz.q: What is the implicit reinvestment rate assumption under the NPV method?
o: Project internal rate of return
Risk-free treasury rate
Firm cost of capital
Zero percent
quiz.why: The NPV technique assumes that intermediate cash inflows can be reinvested at the cost of capital.

quiz.q: In mutually exclusive projects with conflicting rankings between NPV and IRR, which decision rule should prevail?
o: IRR rule because it is a percentage
NPV rule because it maximizes absolute wealth
Payback period rule as a tiebreaker
Average of both rates
quiz.why: The NPV method directly measures total incremental wealth addition for shareholders, making it the superior criterion.

topics.title: Multiple Internal Rates of Return
explain: Conventional cash flows have a single sign change: initial outflow followed by inflows.
Non-conventional cash flows occur when cash flows reverse signs more than once during the project life.
For example, an initial outflow is followed by inflows and later by substantial terminal cleanup outflows.
Each sign reversal can theoretically produce an additional internal rate of return.
In multiple IRR scenarios, the standard IRR rule becomes ambiguous and unreliable.

flow.title: Identifying Multiple IRR Conditions
steps: Track cash flow sequence signs across years
Count the number of sign reversals (+ to - or - to +)
Recognize possibility of multiple discount rates where NPV=0
Discard standard IRR and adopt NPV or MIRR

topics.example: A mining project with an initial setup cost (-), 5 years of mining profits (+), and a massive site restoration cleanup expense in year 6 (-) has two sign changes and potentially two IRRs.
remember: A project can have as many IRRs as there are sign changes in its net cash flow stream.
mistakes: Attempting to use conventional IRR interpolation when cash flows change signs multiple times.

quiz.q: Multiple Internal Rates of Return typically occur when:
o: Cash flows reverse signs during the project life
Cash inflows are perfectly uniform each year
Cost of capital remains completely constant
Project life exceeds 20 years
quiz.why: Non-conventional cash flows that change sign more than once produce multiple roots (multiple IRRs) in the polynomial equation.

quiz.q: Which technique safely resolves the problem of multiple IRRs?
o: Simple Payback Period
Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR) or NPV
Accounting Rate of Return
Payback Reciprocal
quiz.why: MIRR and NPV eliminate multiple rates by discounting negative flows and compounding positive flows at a unique cost of capital.

topics.title: Discounted Payback Period Method
explain: Discounted payback calculates the time needed to recover initial outlays using discounted cash flows.
It overcomes the traditional payback period's limitation of ignoring the time value of money.
Future cash inflows are discounted at the firm's required cost of capital before accumulation.
Discounted payback is always longer than simple undiscounted payback for any positive discount rate.
It still ignores cash inflows occurring after the discounted break-even point is reached.

flow.title: Determining Discounted Payback Period
steps: Determine annual net cash inflows
Discount each annual inflow at required hurdle rate
Accumulate discounted cash flows consecutively
Identify recovery year and add unrecovered fraction

topics.example: A Rs. 30,000 project returning Rs. 6,000 yearly has a simple payback of 5 years, but at a 15% discount rate, the discounted payback is approximately 10 years.
remember: Discounted Payback > Simple Payback whenever discount rate > 0.
Takes time value into account, but still ignores flows beyond recovery.
mistakes: Assuming discounted payback and simple payback will yield the same duration.

quiz.q: Compared to the simple payback period, the discounted payback period will always be:
o: Shorter
Longer (at positive discount rates)
Identical
Unrelated to discount rates
quiz.why: Because discounted cash flows are smaller than nominal flows, it takes more years to accumulate the initial investment.

quiz.q: What deficiency does Discounted Payback share with Simple Payback?
o: It ignores the time value of money
It ignores cash flows generated after the payback period
It requires trial-and-error calculation
It cannot be computed for non-uniform flows
quiz.why: Both methods fail to account for cash flows that occur after the investment has been fully recovered.

topics.title: Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR)
explain: MIRR resolves conventional IRR weaknesses, including multiple IRRs and unrealistic reinvestment rates.
All intermediate cash inflows are compounded forward to the terminal year at the cost of capital.
This compounding produces a single terminal value cash inflow at the end of the project life.
MIRR is the single discount rate equating the initial outlay with the present value of the terminal sum.
Decision rule matches IRR: Accept if MIRR is greater than or equal to the cost of capital.

flow.title: Computing MIRR
steps: Compound all interim inflows to final year at WACC
Sum compounded values to get Terminal Value (TV)
Identify initial investment outlay at Year 0
Solve: Outlay = TV / (1 + MIRR)^n

topics.example: An investment of Rs. 1,36,000 compounds to a terminal value of Rs. 2,13,587 in 5 years at 8%. MIRR = (2,13,587 / 1,36,000)^(1/5) - 1 = 9%.
remember: Formula: MIRR = (Terminal Value / Initial Outlay)^(1/n) - 1.
Reinvestment occurs at WACC, not at project IRR.
mistakes: Compounding the terminal year cash flow for an extra year; Year n inflow compounds for zero years (factor = 1.0).

quiz.q: What reinvestment rate does the Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR) assume for interim cash inflows?
o: The project's MIRR itself
The conventional IRR
The cost of capital
The risk-free rate plus 10%
quiz.why: MIRR reinvests all intermediate cash flows up to the terminal year at the firm's cost of capital.

quiz.q: Why is the MIRR method also known as the Terminal Value method?
o: Because it can only be used when a project terminates abruptly
Because intermediate inflows are compounded forward to a single terminal value
Because it terminates the need for cost of capital calculations
Because it ignores the initial outlay
quiz.why: All future inflows are compounded into a single aggregate terminal value at the project's conclusion.

topics.title: Capital Budgeting under Capital Rationing
explain: Capital rationing occurs when a firm has a hard ceiling on available funds despite positive NPV opportunities.
If projects are divisible (part-project allowed), rank them by NPV per rupee of investment (PI - 1).
Funds are allocated down the ranking order, taking a fractional share of the final project to exhaust funds.
If projects are indivisible, analyze feasible combinations of whole projects within the budget limit.
Select the combination of indivisible projects that produces the maximum total absolute NPV.

flow.title: Capital Rationing Selection Strategy
steps: Check if capital budget is limited
Determine if projects are divisible or indivisible
For divisible: rank by NPV per rupee invested
For indivisible: test combinations within budget
Select project set offering highest aggregate NPV

topics.example: With a Rs. 1,20,000 limit, projects E (Rs. 35k), B (Rs. 40k), C (Rs. 25k) are fully funded, and remaining Rs. 20,000 funds 2/3 of Project D to maximize NPV.
remember: Divisible projects: Rank using NPV per rupee of capital = NPV / Investment.
Indivisible projects: Select feasible project bundle with highest total NPV.
mistakes: Selecting indivisible projects purely by PI rank, which can leave idle cash and yield lower total NPV than another combination.

quiz.q: When independent projects subject to a capital budget constraint are divisible, they should be ranked by:
o: Accounting Rate of Return
Payback period
NPV per rupee of capital investment
Highest initial capital outlay
quiz.why: For divisible projects under rationing, ranking by NPV per rupee of capital generates the maximum total NPV.

quiz.q: If investment projects under capital rationing are indivisible, how should the optimal set be determined?
o: By selecting only the single project with highest IRR
By evaluating feasible combinations within the budget to maximize aggregate NPV
By splitting the budget equally among all available options
By funding the project with the shortest payback period first
quiz.why: Indivisible projects cannot be taken in fractions, so combinations of full projects must be compared to maximize total NPV.

topics.title: Projects with Unequal Lives
explain: Comparing mutually exclusive projects with unequal durations purely on NPV is biased toward longer-lived projects.
Replacement Chain Method replicates projects to a common life (lowest common multiple of years).
Equivalent Annualized Criterion (EAC) converts each project's total NPV into an annual equivalent cash flow.
EAC is computed by dividing the project NPV by the Present Value Annuity Factor (PVAF) for its life.
The project generating the higher Equivalent Annual Benefit (or lowest Equivalent Annual Cost) is selected.

flow.title: Equivalent Annualized Criterion (EAC)
steps: Compute standard project NPV at cost of capital
Find PVAF at cost of capital for project life
Compute EAC = Project NPV / PVAF(k, n)
Select the project with the higher positive EAC

topics.example: Project A (6 yrs) has NPV Rs. 6,49,094 (EAC = 6,49,094/4.112 = Rs. 1,57,854). Project B (3 yrs) has NPV Rs. 5,15,488 (EAC = 5,15,488/2.402 = Rs. 2,14,608). Select Project B.
remember: Equivalent Annualized Inflow = NPV / PVAF(k, n).
Equivalent Annual Cost = Present Value of Total Costs / PVAF(k, n).
mistakes: Directly choosing the project with higher standard NPV without adjusting for different life spans.

quiz.q: Why is a direct comparison of NPV flawed for mutually exclusive projects with unequal useful lives?
o: NPV does not discount cash flows properly
Longer-lived projects accumulate more cash flows and appear artificially superior
Tax depreciation cannot be charged on unequal life assets
Cost of capital changes every year
quiz.why: Standard NPV naturally favors longer project durations because more years of positive cash flows are aggregated.

quiz.q: How is the Equivalent Annualized Criterion calculated from a project's NPV?
o: NPV multiplied by project life in years
NPV divided by the Present Value Annuity Factor for the project's life
NPV divided by the initial investment
NPV multiplied by the salvage value factor
quiz.why: EAC spreads the lump sum NPV evenly across the life of the asset by dividing it by the corresponding PVAF.
